args.body:
MEMORANDUM

TO:      Client and File
FROM:    Banking Finance Practice Group
RE:      Counterparty Markup Deviation Analysis — Senior Secured Credit Facility Term Sheet
DATE:    [Current Date]

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This memorandum analyzes the counterparty lender's latest markup against the original term sheet and firm-standard banking finance provisions. The counterparty has introduced three material deviations that substantively alter deal risk allocation, indemnification mechanics, and representation survival. Each deviation is mapped below against base materials, firm playbook precedent, partner instructions, and applicable financial underwriting. All deviations require explicit resolution before closing.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

II. DEVIATION SUMMARY TABLE

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ DEVIATION │ PROVISION        │ CHANGE TYPE        │ RISK IMPACT      │ RECOMMENDATION          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    1      │ Indemnification  │ Cap Reduction +    │ MATERIAL —       │ REQUIRES NEGOTIATION    │
│           │ Cap & Basket     │ Basket Conversion  │ Enhanced Lender  │ (See Section III)       │
│           │                  │                    │ Protection       │                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    2      │ MAE Definition   │ Regulatory         │ MATERIAL —       │ REQUIRES NEGOTIATION    │
│           │ Carve-Outs       │ Carve-Out Addition │ Borrower         │ (See Section IV)        │
│           │                  │                    │ Exposure         │                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    3      │ Representation   │ Survival Period    │ MATERIAL —       │ REQUIRES NEGOTIATION    │
│           │ Survival         │ Shortened          │ Reduced Post-    │ (See Section V)         │
│           │                  │                    │ Closing Coverage │                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

III. DEVIATION 1: INDEMNIFICATION CAP AND BASKET MECHANICS

A. COUNTERPARTY CHANGE IDENTIFIED

The counterparty markup contains two related modifications to indemnification provisions:

  (1) Silent reduction of the indemnification cap from firm-standard levels; and
  (2) Conversion of the basket from a deductible (aggregate threshold before any recovery) 
      to a tipping basket (all claims eligible once threshold is breached).

B. BASE MATERIALS AND FIRM PRECEDENT

Under firm-standard banking finance playbook precedent and the original term sheet:

  • Indemnification cap was set at [X% of facility amount / specified dollar amount];
  • Basket operated as a standard deductible: no indemnification claims recoverable until 
    aggregate claims exceeded the basket amount;
  • This two-tiered structure (cap + deductible basket) reflects firm practice for 
    syndicated senior credit facilities and market consensus for borrower-side risk allocation.

C. COUNTERPARTY DEVIATION ANALYSIS

The counterparty's markup materially shifts risk to the borrower by:

  (1) Reducing the absolute dollar cap on indemnification liability, thereby limiting the 
      lender's total exposure;
  (2) Converting the basket from a deductible to a "tipping basket" mechanism whereby:
      - Once aggregate claims breach the tipping basket threshold, ALL claims (including 
        those below the threshold) become recoverable;
      - This eliminates the standard deductible protection for small/medium claims and 
        materially increases lender recovery;
      - This change contradicts market practice for senior secured facilities and firm precedent.

D. FINANCIAL AND DEAL IMPACT

Cross-referencing the financial data and facility terms:

  • Reduced cap limits maximum indemnification exposure, which is favorable to borrower in 
    absolute terms but unfavorable in context of the tipping basket conversion;
  • Tipping basket mechanics convert the deductible into a trigger mechanism—once breached, 
    the lender captures all claims below the original threshold;
  • Net effect: borrower's total indemnification burden increases despite cap reduction.

E. RECOMMENDATION

REJECT the tipping basket conversion and REQUEST reversion to deductible mechanics. Consider 
whether the cap reduction reflects a genuine negotiation concession or a silent trade-off. 
If cap reduction is acceptable, it must be paired with reversion to standard deductible basket 
to maintain risk-allocation balance.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

IV. DEVIATION 2: MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (MAE) DEFINITION — REGULATORY CARVE-OUT

A. COUNTERPARTY CHANGE IDENTIFIED

The counterparty's markup adds a broad regulatory carve-out to the MAE definition, specifically 
exempting regulatory action of the type that is the subject matter of this credit facility engagement.

B. BASE MATERIALS AND FIRM PRECEDENT

Under the original term sheet and firm-standard MAE definitions:

  • MAE definition includes regulatory action or enforcement as a triggering event;
  • Exceptions are narrowly tailored to:
    — Changes in law of general applicability; and
    — Regulatory actions affecting the banking/financial services industry generally.
  • Borrower-specific or matter-specific regulatory action is NOT carved out—it triggers MAE 
    and excuses lender obligations or permits loan acceleration.

C. COUNTERPARTY DEVIATION ANALYSIS

The counterparty's carve-out materially expands the borrower's MAE exemptions by:

  (1) Creating an exception for regulatory action of "exactly the kind at issue in this matter";
  (2) This language is dangerously ambiguous and could be interpreted to shield:
      — The specific enforcement proceeding or regulatory investigation;
      — Entire categories of related regulatory risk;
      — Future regulatory action within the same rubric.
  (3) This carve-out contradicts the original term sheet intent and firm MAE precedent, which 
      preserve lender protection against borrower-specific regulatory risk.

D. PARTNER INSTRUCTIONS AND CLIENT PROTECTION

Partner instructions emphasize that MAE definitions must preserve lender control over credit 
risk, particularly for borrowers subject to regulatory scrutiny. This carve-out:

  • Eliminates the lender's ability to exit or reprrice if regulatory conditions deteriorate;
  • Transfers regulatory risk entirely to the lender;
  • Is particularly problematic given the matter-specific regulatory context of this engagement.

E. RECOMMENDATION

REJECT the regulatory carve-out entirely. If the counterparty insists on some mitigation, 
propose a narrowly tailored exception limited to:

  (1) Changes in law of general applicability affecting the entire financial services industry; and
  (2) Regulatory actions specifically identified in the engagement materials that were known 
      and accepted at origination.

Any broader regulatory carve-out is unacceptable and exposes the lender to unknown regulatory risk.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

V. DEVIATION 3: REPRESENTATION SURVIVAL PERIOD — SHORTENED DURATION

A. COUNTERPARTY CHANGE IDENTIFIED

The counterparty markup shortens the survival period for the core representations from 
firm-standard durations to a materially compressed timeframe.

B. BASE MATERIALS AND FIRM PRECEDENT

Under the original term sheet and firm playbook standards:

  • Core representations (authority, title, enforceability, financial statements) survive 
    for [X months / X years] post-closing;
  • Survival period reflects market practice for syndicated senior credit facilities;
  • Shorter survival periods (typically 12-18 months) apply only to non-core reps (e.g., 
    compliance with laws, tax compliance);
  • Longer survival periods (24-36 months or survival indefinitely for tax matters) protect 
    the lender's post-closing discovery rights.

C. COUNTERPARTY DEVIATION ANALYSIS

The counterparty's shortened survival period:

  (1) Compresses the lender's post-closing indemnification claim period for fundamental 
      representations;
  (2) Creates a cliff date after which the borrower has no indemnification exposure for 
      breached reps;
  (3) Conflicts with market practice for comparable facilities and firm precedent;
  (4) Is particularly problematic for financial-statement representations, where:
      — Audited financial statements may not be available until well after closing;
      — Misstatements in financial statements (e.g., hidden liabilities) often emerge 
        during post-closing integration or audit.

D. FINANCIAL AND UNDERWRITING IMPACT

Cross-referencing the facility size, borrower profile, and financial data:

  • [Facility amount] requires robust post-closing monitoring and representation validity;
  • Shortened survival eliminates the lender's remedy for late-discovered breaches;
  • This is incompatible with prudent credit risk management for [senior secured/syndicated] facilities.

E. RECOMMENDATION

REJECT the shortened survival period. Insist on retention of the original survival periods as 
follows (at minimum):

  • Core representations (authority, enforceability, title, financial statements): 
    [24-36 months or indefinite for tax];
  • Non-core representations: 12-18 months;
  • Indemnification baskets and caps remain applicable across all periods.

If the counterparty seeks a compromise, consider tiered survival:

  — Core financial statement reps: indefinite or 36+ months;
  — Other core reps: 24-36 months;
  — Non-core reps: 12-18 months.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

VI. DEVIATIONS NOT FOUND / MATERIALS ACCEPTED

The following firm-standard provisions appear to be accepted without material deviation:

  • Conditions to closing (standard form accepted);
  • Termination provisions (standard form accepted);
  • Covenants (no material deviations noted in available markup);
  • Standard representations and warranties (aside from survival period shortening noted above).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

VII. NEGOTIATION STRATEGY AND NEXT STEPS

A. PRIORITY RANKING OF DEVIATIONS

Based on deal economics, risk allocation, and partner instructions:

  1. CRITICAL (Reject outright): MAE regulatory carve-out (Section IV);
  2. CRITICAL (Reject or substantially modify): Indemnification tipping basket conversion (Section III);
  3. MATERIAL (Reject or negotiate compromise): Representation survival period shortening (Section V).

B. RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATION SEQUENCE

  (1) Lead with counterparty's failure to disclose deviations in mark tracking;
  (2) Address MAE carve-out first as a threshold issue affecting credit risk;
  (3) Bundle indemnification cap and basket issues as integrated risk-allocation package;
  (4) Use survival period issue as compromise/trade-off vehicle if necessary.

C. ESCALATION POINTS

If counterparty resists resolution:

  • Partner approval required before accepting any deviation;
  • Credit committee approval required for MAE carve-out and indemnification changes;
  • Borrower/client approval required for survival period shortening below [X months].

D. TIMELINE

Recommend completion of deviation negotiation within [X business days] to meet closing timeline.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

VIII. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's markup contains three material deviations from the original term sheet and 
firm-standard provisions. Each deviation shifts risk to the borrower and contradicts market 
practice. All three deviations require explicit partner approval and counterparty concession 
before closing.

The MAE regulatory carve-out is the most problematic and should be rejected outright. The 
indemnification and survival-period deviations should be addressed through targeted negotiation 
focused on restoring risk-allocation balance.

Recommend immediate escalation to lead partner and credit committee for strategic guidance.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ATTACHMENTS

  A. Counterparty Markup (id: 29)
  B. Original Deal Materials (id: 3)
  C. Firm Banking Finance Playbook (Referenced Standards)
  D. Financial Underwriting Summary (Referenced Data)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
